section.title: The Sabbath and the Offering
section.sectionRationale: After the covenant is renewed, construction of the tabernacle finally begins. Moses restates the Sabbath command to the assembled congregation, then calls for a freewill offering, and the people respond with overflowing generosity, presenting Bezalel and Oholiab as the Spirit-gifted craftsmen who will lead the work.
section.thesis: Moses gathers Israel, restates the Sabbath, and calls for a willing offering for the tabernacle, and the people, men and women alike, give so generously and skillfully that the LORD's chosen craftsmen, Bezalel and Oholiab, are ready to begin building.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the Sabbath restated to the whole congregation; the call for offerings of materials and skilled labor; the people's overflowing, willing response; and the announcement of Bezalel and Oholiab, filled with the Spirit for the work.

units.label: The Sabbath restated
units.note: a holy day, a Sabbath of complete rest

verses.text: Then Moses assembled the whole congregation of Israel and said to them, “These are the things that the LORD has commanded you to do:
For six days work may be done, but the seventh day shall be your holy day, a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD. Whoever does any work on that day must be put to death.
Do not light a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day.”

media.alt: Hands offering gold, yarn, and wood
media.caption: Moses calls for a willing offering to build everything the LORD has commanded.

verses.text: Moses also told the whole congregation of Israel, “This is what the LORD has commanded:
Take from among you an offering to the LORD. Let everyone whose heart is {{willing|willing}} bring an offering to the LORD: gold, silver, and bronze;
blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair;
ram skins dyed red and fine leather; acacia wood;
olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense;
and onyx stones and gemstones to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece.
Let every skilled craftsman among you come and make everything that the LORD has commanded:
the tabernacle with its tent and covering, its clasps and frames, its crossbars, posts, and bases;
the ark with its poles and mercy seat, and the veil to shield it;
the table with its poles, all its utensils, and the Bread of the Presence;
the lampstand for light with its accessories and lamps and oil for the light;
the altar of incense with its poles; the anointing oil and fragrant incense; the curtain for the doorway at the entrance to the tabernacle;
the altar of burnt offering with its bronze grate, its poles, and all its utensils; the basin with its stand;
the curtains of the courtyard with its posts and bases, and the curtain for the gate of the courtyard;
the tent pegs for the tabernacle and for the courtyard, along with their ropes;
and the woven garments for ministering in the holy place, both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons to serve as priests.”
Then the whole congregation of Israel withdrew from the presence of Moses.
And everyone whose heart stirred him and whose spirit prompted him came and brought an offering to the LORD for the work on the Tent of Meeting, for all its services, and for the holy garments.

So all who had willing hearts, both men and women, came and brought brooches and earrings, rings and necklaces, and all kinds of gold jewelry. And they all presented their gold as a wave offering to the LORD.
Everyone who had blue, purple, or scarlet yarn, or fine linen, goat hair, ram skins dyed red, or articles of fine leather, brought them.
And all who could present an offering of silver or bronze brought it as a contribution to the LORD. Also, everyone who had acacia wood for any part of the service brought it.
Every skilled woman spun with her hands and brought what she had spun: blue, purple, or scarlet yarn, or fine linen.
And all the skilled women whose hearts were stirred spun the goat hair.
The leaders brought onyx stones and gemstones to mount on the ephod and breastpiece,
as well as spices and olive oil for the light, for the anointing oil, and for the fragrant incense.
So all the men and women of the Israelites whose hearts prompted them brought a freewill offering to the LORD for all the work that the LORD through Moses had commanded them to do.

units.label: Bezalel and Oholiab announced
units.note: filled with the Spirit of God

verses.text: Then Moses said to the Israelites, “See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
And He has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship,
to design artistic works in gold, silver, and bronze,
to cut gemstones for settings, and to carve wood, so that he may be a master of every artistic craft.
And the LORD has given both him and Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, the {{ability|ability}} to teach others.

He has filled them with skill to do all kinds of work as engravers, designers, embroiderers in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen, and as weavers, as artistic designers of every kind of craft.

willing.gloss: A willing, or generous, heart. This phrase, repeated throughout the chapter, describes the freely stirred motivation behind Israel's giving, offerings given from love and eagerness rather than command or compulsion.

ability.gloss: The ability to teach or instruct. Bezalel and Oholiab were not only gifted craftsmen themselves but given the further gift of passing their skill to others, ensuring the work could be carried out by many hands, not theirs alone.

basic.context: With the covenant renewed, Moses gathers all Israel, restates the Sabbath, and calls for a freewill offering of materials and skilled labor to build the tabernacle. The people respond so generously, men and women alike bringing gold, yarn, wood, and their own skilled handiwork, that Moses can announce Bezalel and Oholiab, filled with God's Spirit, as ready to lead the work.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a historical account of Israel's actual response to God's call for the tabernacle's construction. Its significance lies not in hidden symbolism but in what it plainly shows: genuine, willing generosity flowing from a people whose hearts had been stirred, contrasted sharply with the golden calf's earlier, misdirected generosity toward an idol.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter repeats nadiv lev, willing or generous heart, again and again, emphasizing that true worship flows from a heart moved, not merely a rule obeyed. Bezalel and Oholiab receive not only skill but horaah, the ability to teach others, so that the Spirit's gifting would multiply through many hands.
basic.typology: The people's overflowing, willing generosity for God's true dwelling place stands in deliberate contrast with their earlier eager giving toward the golden calf, showing that the same generous impulse can be directed rightly or wrongly. This redirected generosity anticipates the cheerful giving Paul commends among believers building up the true temple of God's people.
basic.christ: Paul writes that God loves a cheerful giver, 2 Corinthians 9:7, echoing exactly the willing-hearted giving described throughout this chapter. The skilled craftsmen equipped to build God's earthly dwelling anticipate the gifted members of Christ's body, equipped by the same Spirit to build up the church, His true temple, Ephesians 4:11-13.
basic.god: God does not merely command Israel's generosity; He first stirs their hearts, so that giving flows from willingness rather than obligation. He also multiplies His gifting, giving not only skill to Bezalel and Oholiab but the further ability to teach, ensuring His work is carried forward by many rather than a gifted few.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Corinthians 9:7 says God loves a cheerful giver. Ephesians 4:11-13 describes gifted members equipping the whole body of Christ for the work of ministry. 1 Peter 4:10 calls every believer to use whatever gift they have received to serve others.
basic.oneStory: Israel's hearts, once misdirected toward a golden calf, are now stirred to overflowing generosity for God's true dwelling place, and the Spirit equips craftsmen not only with skill but the ability to teach others. This pattern of Spirit-stirred, willing giving and Spirit-multiplied gifting continues in the church, the true temple, built up by every believer's freely offered gifts.

context.literary:
Exodus 35 opens the last major block of the book. Chapters 35 to 40 report the carrying out of the instructions given in chapters 25 to 31, often repeating them almost word for word, and the repetition is the point. Everything God commanded on the mountain is now done exactly, until 'Moses finished the work,' Exodus 40:33.

The order of the instructions has been reversed. The Sabbath came last in the original commands, Exodus 31:12-17, and it comes first here, verses 1 to 3. The two Sabbath passages form a frame around the story of the calf and the renewal of the covenant. Whatever happened in between, the building of God's house begins and ends inside His rest.

The chapter's first verb matters too. 'Moses assembled the whole congregation,' verse 1, uses the same verb as Exodus 32:1, where the people 'gathered around Aaron' to demand gods. The first assembly produced a calf; this one produces a sanctuary.

The chapter moves in four steps: the Sabbath command, verses 1 to 3; Moses' call for materials and craftsmen, verses 4 to 19; the people's response, verses 20 to 29; and the announcement of Bezalel and Oholiab, verses 30 to 35. The long lists slow the reader down. The materials in verses 5 to 9 and the items in verses 11 to 19 repeat the inventory of the earlier chapters, and they will be repeated again as the work is done. Like a liturgy, they invite lingering over each object.

Two words run through the chapter as refrains. One is 'heart': a willing heart, verse 5 and 22, a heart that stirred, verse 21 and 26, and skill described literally as wisdom of heart, verses 10, 25 and 35. The other is 'work,' the word used for the Sabbath prohibition in verse 2 and then for the building of the tent in verses 21, 24, 29, 31, 33 and 35. The same word describes God's own work of creation in Genesis 2:2-3.

The account of Bezalel, verses 30 to 35, repeats Exodus 31:1-6 with one significant addition. He and Oholiab are given the ability 'to teach others,' verse 34.
context.historical:
The materials describe the wealth of a people recently freed from slavery. Much of it had come from Egypt, where Israel asked the Egyptians for 'articles of silver and gold, and for clothing,' Exodus 12:35. The dyes were costly. Blue and purple were commonly obtained from sea snails in the ancient world, and scarlet from an insect dye, so that coloured yarn was a mark of royalty and wealth. Fine linen was a well known product of Egypt. Acacia wood, by contrast, grew in the Sinai wilderness itself, and goat hair was the ordinary material of nomadic tents. The BSB footnote to verse 7 notes that 'fine leather' may refer to the hides of large sea creatures.

Spinning, verses 25 and 26, was ordinary household work for women in the ancient Near East, and here it becomes a sacred contribution. The text is careful to include women repeatedly, verses 22, 25, 26 and 29, and later records that the bronze basin was made from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, Exodus 38:8.

Bezalel's family was prominent. His grandfather Hur had held up Moses' hands in the battle with Amalek, Exodus 17:10-12, and had shared leadership with Aaron while Moses was on the mountain, Exodus 24:14. The Chronicler places him in the line of Judah, 1 Chronicles 2:20. His name is usually understood as 'in the shadow of God.' Oholiab came from Dan, a tribe that marched last as the rear guard of the camp, Numbers 10:25. His name is usually taken as 'the Father is my tent,' fitting for a builder of God's tent.

The Sabbath law in verses 2 and 3 carries the death penalty stated in Exodus 31:14-15. The ban on lighting a fire in every dwelling is stated here explicitly for the first time. In a world without matches, kindling a fire meant gathering fuel and labour, and Numbers 15:32-36 records a man executed for gathering wood on the Sabbath.
context.canonical:
The chapter's two themes, Sabbath and willing offering, both run through the rest of Scripture.

The Sabbath goes back to the seventh day of creation, Genesis 2:2-3, and was given to Israel with the manna before Sinai, Exodus 16:23-29. The commandment grounds it in creation, Exodus 20:8-11, and Deuteronomy adds the exodus, 'Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt,' Deuteronomy 5:15. The prophets treat Sabbath keeping as a test of covenant loyalty, Jeremiah 17:21-22 and Isaiah 58:13, and after the exile Nehemiah confronts traders who worked on the Sabbath, Nehemiah 13:15. Jesus declares that 'the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath,' and that He is 'Lord even of the Sabbath,' Mark 2:27-28. Paul calls the Sabbath 'a shadow of the things to come,' Colossians 2:16-17, and Hebrews speaks of 'a Sabbath rest for the people of God' that remains, Hebrews 4:9-10.

The willing offering for God's house is repeated when David prepares for the temple. The people give 'freely and wholeheartedly,' and David prays, 'from Your own hand we have given to You,' 1 Chronicles 29:9 and 29:14. The exiles who return to rebuild are helped with gifts 'in addition to all their freewill offerings,' Ezra 1:6.

Bezalel's gifts are echoed in the building of Solomon's temple. Huram of Tyre had 'great skill, understanding, and knowledge,' 1 Kings 7:14, the same three gifts named in verse 31. The Chronicler adds that Huram's mother was 'from the daughters of Dan,' 2 Chronicles 2:14, so that the temple, like the tabernacle, was built with skill from Dan. The bronze altar Bezalel made still stood at Gibeon in Solomon's day, 2 Chronicles 1:5.

In the New Testament, Paul urges the Corinthians to give as the Macedonians did, 'of their own accord,' 2 Corinthians 8:3-5, and roots all Christian giving in the grace of Christ, 2 Corinthians 8:9. The pattern of the Spirit gifting many hands for one building reappears in the church, where 'there are different gifts, but the same Spirit,' 1 Corinthians 12:4, and believers are 'being built together into a dwelling place for God,' Ephesians 2:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that the forgiven people were now doing what the unfaithful people had failed to do. The last time Israel assembled, they gave gold for a calf, Exodus 32:2-3. Now they assemble to give gold for God's dwelling, and they give it in the way He asked. The book is showing a people restored to their calling.

He placed the Sabbath first to remind them whose work this was. Even the most sacred labour, building the sanctuary, stops on the seventh day. The tabernacle was not a human achievement to be pushed forward at any cost; it was a gift of God to be built within the rhythm He set. Israel was meant to learn that holy work does not override holy rest.

He wanted them to understand that God's house would be built by the whole people. Men and women, leaders and ordinary households, the skilled spinner and the man with acacia wood all have a part, verses 22 to 29. No one is excluded from contributing, and no gift is too humble.

He also meant them to see that skill is a gift of God's Spirit. The ability to cut stones, carve wood and weave cloth is described in the same language as the Spirit's work in creation, verse 31. Craft, art and design are not second rate compared with prophecy or leadership. When they serve God's purposes, they are the Spirit's work.

Finally, the addition in verse 34, the ability to teach, told Israel that God's gifts are meant to be passed on. A master craftsman who trains others multiplies the work beyond his own hands.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The Sabbath command in verses 2 and 3, with its death penalty and its ban on lighting a fire, was given to Israel as the sign of the Sinai covenant, Exodus 31:13. The New Testament does not apply it to the church in that form. Christians have differed on how the principle of a day of rest carries over, but none take the penalty as binding, and Paul warns against letting anyone judge believers 'with regard to a Sabbath,' Colossians 2:16.

The collection of materials was for a specific building at a specific time, and it came to an end when the people brought more than enough, Exodus 36:5-7. It is not a direct command about church buildings or budgets. What it describes, however, is the right spirit for all giving to God: willing, from what one has, prompted by a stirred heart. Paul teaches the same, 'not out of regret or compulsion,' 2 Corinthians 9:7, and 'according to what one has,' 2 Corinthians 8:12.

The filling of Bezalel with the Spirit is also described rather than commanded. No believer is promised Bezalel's particular skills. But the passage does teach that practical gifts of making and teaching come from God and are to be used for His purposes, as Peter says of every gift, 1 Peter 4:10.

debates.question: Does this chapter's emphasis on 'whoever has a willing heart' teach that giving to God's work should always be entirely voluntary, with no expectation or structure at all?

views.label: Voluntary giving as the ideal pattern
views.case: Many interpreters see this passage, alongside 2 Corinthians 9:7, as establishing that giving to God's work is meant to flow from a freely stirred heart rather than compulsion, making this freewill offering a positive model for Christian giving generally.

views.label: Voluntary alongside other required giving
views.case: Others note that Israel also had required tithes and offerings elsewhere in the law, so this passage's voluntary character was specific to this particular building project, not a claim that all giving under the law was optional; the New Testament likewise combines cheerful, voluntary giving with expectations of regular, sacrificial generosity.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm that the heart behind giving matters deeply to God, whether or not every instance of giving in Scripture was strictly voluntary; willingness and cheerfulness are consistently commended as the right spirit behind any giving.

debates.question: Does the Sabbath command of verses 2 and 3 still bind Christians?

views.label: Fulfilled in Christ and not binding as a day
views.case: Many hold that the Sabbath was the sign of the Sinai covenant, Exodus 31:13, and that its substance is Christ. Paul lists it among things that are 'a shadow of the things to come,' Colossians 2:16-17, and allows believers to differ over days, Romans 14:5. The rest it pictured is found in Christ, Matthew 11:28 and Hebrews 4:9-10, so no weekly day is required.

views.label: A creation pattern carried into the Lord's day
views.case: Others note that the Sabbath rests on creation, Genesis 2:2-3 and Exodus 20:11, not only on Sinai, and so reflects a lasting pattern of six days' work and one day's rest. The church met on the first day of the week, Acts 20:7, and John speaks of 'the Lord's day,' Revelation 1:10. On this view the principle continues, transferred to the day of resurrection, while the penalties of verse 2 belonged to Israel's civil law.

views.label: The seventh day still to be kept
views.case: A smaller number of Christians hold that the fourth commandment, as part of the Ten Words, continues unchanged, including its day. They point to Jesus' own Sabbath observance and to the creation grounding of the command.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the Sabbath teaches that human work is not ultimate and that rest is a gift from God. They differ over how that gift is received under the new covenant. The capital penalty and the ban on fire were tied to Israel's covenant life and are not applied to the church by any mainstream view.

debates.question: Is the Spirit's filling of Bezalel the same as the gift of the Spirit in the New Testament?

views.label: A special empowering for a particular task
views.case: In the Old Testament the Spirit often comes on particular people for particular work: on the seventy elders to prophesy, Numbers 11:25, on judges for deliverance, Judges 14:6, and on Bezalel for craftsmanship. On this view Bezalel's filling was an equipping for the tabernacle, not the indwelling promised to all believers in the new covenant, Ezekiel 36:26-27.

views.label: The same Spirit, now given more widely
views.case: Others stress continuity. It is the same Spirit of God, and the New Testament also describes practical gifts such as serving, giving and leading, Romans 12:6-8. What changes at Pentecost is not the nature of the Spirit's gifting but its breadth, poured out 'on all people,' sons and daughters alike, Acts 2:17-18.

debates.bearing: Both views are partly right. The pattern of Bezalel shows how the Spirit equips for service, and that pattern continues. The new covenant adds what Bezalel's filling did not include: the Spirit dwelling in every believer and making them together the house of God, 1 Corinthians 3:16.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter opens with vayyaqhel, 'Moses assembled,' from qahal, to gather or assemble. The same verb described the people who 'gathered around Aaron' in Exodus 32:1. The related noun qahal, assembly or congregation, is often rendered in the Septuagint with ekklesia, the word the New Testament uses for the church, and Stephen calls Israel at Sinai 'the assembly in the wilderness,' Acts 7:38. The chapter is about what an assembly gathered by God does, in contrast to one gathered against Him.

Verse 2 calls the seventh day 'a Sabbath of complete rest,' shabbat shabbaton. Hebrew often forms a superlative by repeating a word in related forms, and this phrase means the most complete rest. It is used also of the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:31, and of the weekly Sabbath in Leviticus 23:3 and Exodus 31:15.

The word for 'work' in verse 2 is melakhah, the ordinary noun for skilled labour or business. It is the very word Genesis uses for God's work of creation, 'the work He had been doing,' Genesis 2:2. The same noun then recurs throughout the chapter for the building of the tabernacle, verses 21, 24, 29, 31, 33 and 35. The juxtaposition is deliberate. The work of building God's dwelling is the most honoured melakhah in Israel, yet it too must stop on the seventh day.

The 'offering' of verse 5 is terumah, from the root rum, to be high or to lift. It refers to what is lifted off or set apart from one's possessions for God, the same word used in the first call for materials, Exodus 25:2. The 'wave offering' of verse 22, tenufah, comes from a verb meaning to wave or swing, a gesture of presenting a gift before the LORD.

In verse 21 the BSB says 'everyone whose heart stirred him.' The Hebrew reads literally 'whose heart lifted him,' using nasa, the verb that in Exodus 34:7 describes God lifting away iniquity. In verse 29 the gifts are a nedavah, a 'freewill offering,' from the same root as the willing heart of verse 5. The root describes spontaneous, self-moved giving. It appears in the Song of Deborah, 'when the people volunteer,' Judges 5:2, in Psalm 110:3, 'Your people shall be willing,' and in David's prayer for 'a willing spirit,' Psalm 51:12.

The craftsmen are described as 'skilled,' chakham lev, literally 'wise of heart,' verses 10 and 25, and God 'has filled them with skill,' literally wisdom of heart, verse 35. In the Old Testament chokhmah, wisdom, is first of all practical expertise, the skill of a craftsman or a sailor, before it is moral insight. In verse 31 God fills Bezalel with chokhmah, tevunah and da'at, 'skill, ability, and knowledge.' The same triad describes God's own work in creation: 'The LORD founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding. By His knowledge the watery depths were broken open,' Proverbs 3:19-20. And the phrase 'the Spirit of God,' ruach elohim, is the phrase of Genesis 1:2. Bezalel builds God's house with the gifts by which God built the world.

Finally, verse 34 says literally that God 'has put in his heart to teach,' using the verb yarah, to teach or instruct, the root from which torah, instruction, is formed. The gift of teaching is set in the same heart where the gift of skill resides.

typology.type: Bezalel of Judah, called by name and filled with the Spirit to build God's dwelling, Exodus 35:30-31
typology.fulfillment: Bezalel comes from Judah, is filled with the Spirit of God, and builds the place where God will dwell among His people. Isaiah promises a son of David on whom the Spirit 'will rest,' 'the Spirit of wisdom and understanding,' Isaiah 11:2, and Jesus, of the tribe of Judah, receives the Spirit 'without limit,' John 3:34. He speaks of His own body as the temple He will raise, John 2:19-21, and says 'I will build My church,' Matthew 16:18. The escalation is that Bezalel built with materials others supplied, while Christ builds His house by giving Himself. Bezalel's tent was taken down; Christ's building grows into a holy temple, Ephesians 2:21.

typology.type: The Sabbath placed before the building begins, Exodus 35:1-3
typology.fulfillment: Israel's work on God's house had to begin from rest and pause for rest, for the Sabbath was God's sign that He is the One who sanctifies, Exodus 31:13. Jesus invites the weary to come to Him for rest, Matthew 11:28, and calls Himself 'Lord even of the Sabbath,' Mark 2:28. Hebrews says a Sabbath rest remains for God's people, in which they rest from their own works as God did from His, Hebrews 4:9-10. The type falls short because the weekly Sabbath had to be kept again and again under threat of death; the rest Christ gives is a settled peace with God that the seventh day only pictured.

typology.type: Many hands and many materials woven into one dwelling for God, Exodus 35:21-29
typology.fulfillment: Gold from the leaders, yarn spun by women, wood from ordinary households, all become one tabernacle. Peter describes believers as 'living stones' being 'built into a spiritual house,' 1 Peter 2:5, and Paul says the whole building 'is fitted together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord,' Ephesians 2:21-22. The escalation is that the people are no longer simply donors to God's house; they are its materials, indwelt by God's Spirit, 1 Corinthians 3:16. Even members that seem weaker are indispensable, 1 Corinthians 12:22, as Dan's craftsman was set beside Judah's.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ first through its framing command. The building of God's house begins with the Sabbath, and the Gospels show Jesus as the One who brings the Sabbath's meaning to light. He declares, 'The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath,' Mark 2:27-28. When challenged for healing on the Sabbath, He answers, 'To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working,' John 5:17. The One who gives rest is also the One whose work never ceases. And the rest He offers, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary,' Matthew 11:28, is what the Sabbath of complete rest was always pointing toward.

It points to Christ through the Spirit-filled builder. Bezalel, of Judah, is filled with the Spirit of God with wisdom, understanding and knowledge. Isaiah says the coming son of David will have 'the Spirit of wisdom and understanding' and 'the Spirit of knowledge,' Isaiah 11:2. At Nazareth Jesus reads, 'The Spirit of the Lord is on Me,' Luke 4:18. The Gospels also remember that He was a craftsman, 'the carpenter,' Mark 6:3. More deeply, He is the builder of the true house of God. Hebrews says He 'has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself,' Hebrews 3:3.

It points to Christ as the ground of all willing giving. The people of Israel gave because their hearts had been stirred after God forgave them. Paul roots Christian generosity in the same place, but with a deeper motive: 'you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. Israel gave gold and linen out of what God had given them from Egypt. Christ gave Himself.

It points to Christ as the giver of gifts for building. The Spirit who filled Bezalel and gave him the ability to teach is the Spirit whom the ascended Christ pours out. Paul quotes Psalm 68 to say that 'when He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men,' Ephesians 4:7-8. The craftsmen of Exodus 35 were gifted by God for the tabernacle; the members of Christ's body are gifted by Christ for His church.

Restraint keeps the reading honest. The colours of the yarn, the onyx stones and the acacia wood are not coded prophecies of Christ, and Scripture does not treat them so. The links lie in the Sabbath He fulfils, the Spirit He bears and gives, the house He builds, and the grace from which all willing giving flows.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who is both Lord of work and Giver of rest. The seventh day is 'your holy day, a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD,' verse 2. God claims one day in seven as His own, and in doing so He sets limits on human labour. Even the construction of His own dwelling must pause. God is not so eager for His house that He will exhaust His people to build it. His holiness includes His care for their rest.

He is the God who asks for gifts and yet needs nothing. 'Take from among you an offering to the LORD,' verse 5, comes from the God who says, 'the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof,' Psalm 50:12. Paul makes the point directly: He is not 'served by human hands, as if He needed anything,' Acts 17:25. God invites His people's gifts because it is good for them to give, and because He delights to build His house with their willing participation. David understood this: 'from Your own hand we have given to You,' 1 Chronicles 29:14.

He is the God who moves hearts. The offering is brought by those 'whose heart stirred him and whose spirit prompted him,' verse 21. The text does not explain how, but the whole flow of Exodus 32 to 35 suggests that the stirring came from the experience of forgiveness. God does not extract gifts by pressure. He changes people so that they want to give.

He is a God who values beauty and skill. The chapter is full of 'artistic works,' 'every artistic craft,' 'designers' and 'embroiderers,' verses 32 to 35. God did not ask for a plain shelter. He asked for gold, colour, gemstones and fine weaving, and He gave the skill to make them. The same God who made a world 'very good,' Genesis 1:31, wants His dwelling to be beautiful.

He is the God who calls individuals by name. 'See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel,' verse 30. The phrase echoes God's words to Israel, 'I have called you by your name; you are Mine,' Isaiah 43:1. God's great purposes are carried out through particular people He has chosen and known.

He fills with His Spirit for ordinary tasks. The Spirit of God who hovered over the waters at creation, Genesis 1:2, is the Spirit who guides a craftsman's hands. God's work in the world is not confined to the dramatic. It includes the carving of wood and the cutting of stones.

And He multiplies His gifts through teaching, verse 34, so that the skill He gives to one becomes the skill of many. For worship, the chapter calls believers to bring what they have, to use what they have been given, and to rest when God says rest, trusting that the house is His and He will see it built. As Moses prayed, 'establish the work of our hands,' Psalm 90:17.

crossReferences.note: The Sabbath command that closed the original instructions, now restated to open their execution. It calls the Sabbath 'a sign between Me and you' and grounds it in God's own rest after creation. Together the two passages frame the calf and the renewal, so that the whole crisis sits within God's rest.

The earlier call for gold. Aaron told the people to take off their earrings, and they brought them eagerly for the calf. Exodus 35:22 describes the people bringing 'brooches and earrings' again, but this time to God, in the way He asked, for the dwelling He designed.

The sequel to this chapter. The craftsmen tell Moses the people are bringing 'more than enough,' and a proclamation goes through the camp to stop the giving. The giving has to be restrained rather than urged, which shows how deeply their hearts had been stirred.

A man is found gathering wood on the Sabbath and is put to death at the LORD's command. The case shows how seriously the prohibition of Exodus 35:2-3 was taken, including the preparation of fire, and why the Sabbath functioned as a test of loyalty to the covenant.

God founded the earth 'by wisdom,' established the heavens 'by understanding,' and broke open the depths 'by His knowledge.' These are the three gifts given to Bezalel in Exodus 35:31, skill, ability and knowledge. The craftsman of the tabernacle works with the gifts by which God made the world.

David's preparation for the temple repeats the pattern of the tabernacle offering. The leaders give freely and wholeheartedly, the people rejoice, and David confesses that 'everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.' Willing gifts for God's house are always gifts returned.

Huram-abi, the master craftsman sent for Solomon's temple, is 'the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan,' skilled in gold, silver, bronze, coloured yarn and fine linen. The temple, like the tabernacle, is built with skill that traces back to Dan, the tribe of Oholiab.

Paul holds up the Macedonians, who gave 'of their own accord' and 'gave themselves first to the Lord,' and then grounds all giving in the grace of Christ, who became poor for our sakes. The willing hearts of Exodus 35 are here given their deepest motive.

Paul describes a variety of gifts, ministries and ways of working, all from 'the same Spirit' and given 'for the common good.' It is the church's version of Exodus 35, where the same Spirit equips different people with different skills to build one dwelling for God.

The writer says a Sabbath rest remains for God's people, in which those who enter God's rest cease from their own works as God did from His. The Sabbath of complete rest in Exodus 35:2 is taken as a picture of the final rest believers enter through faith.

At Pentecost Peter announces that God is pouring out His Spirit 'on all people,' sons and daughters, menservants and maidservants. What was given to Bezalel and Oholiab for one building is now given to the whole people of God, men and women alike, as the church is built.

study.oneStory:
Exodus 35 quietly retells creation. In the beginning the Spirit of God hovered over the waters, Genesis 1:2, and God worked six days and rested on the seventh, Genesis 2:2-3. Here the Spirit of God fills a craftsman, verse 31, the people are told to work six days and rest on the seventh, verse 2, and the work of building begins. When the tabernacle is finished, the language of Genesis returns. Moses sees that the work was done 'just as the LORD had commanded' and blesses the people, Exodus 39:43, echoing God seeing that His work was very good, Genesis 1:31, and 'Moses finished the work,' Exodus 40:33, echoes God finishing His work, Genesis 2:2. The tabernacle is a small world where God dwells with His people, a picture of what creation was meant to be.

The chapter also answers the fall that happened at Sinai. Israel's gold went into a calf, and their assembly around Aaron produced an idol. Now the same people, forgiven, bring their gold to God and assemble to build His house. The story of redemption is a story of restored worship, of human gifts and skills redirected to their proper end.

The pattern continues through Israel's history. David and the people give freely for the temple, 1 Chronicles 29:9, and Solomon's builder carries skill from Dan, 2 Chronicles 2:14. After the exile, the returning people bring freewill offerings to rebuild, Ezra 1:6, and the prophet reminds them that the house will be finished 'not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit,' Zechariah 4:6.

In Christ the building moves to its true centre. He speaks of His own body as the temple, John 2:21. Through His death and resurrection He gives His Spirit to all His people, Acts 2:17-18, and they become together 'a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22. Their gifts, their giving and their work are now the materials of God's house.

The story ends in a city that is itself God's dwelling. John sees a city of 'pure gold' with foundations 'adorned with every kind of precious stone,' Revelation 21:18-19, the gold and gemstones of Exodus 35 on a cosmic scale. Into it 'the glory and honor of the nations' will be brought, Revelation 21:26, the willing offerings of a redeemed humanity. And there 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3, the purpose for which the tabernacle was first built, now fulfilled forever in a Sabbath rest that never ends.

quiz.q: What did Moses restate to the whole congregation at the beginning of this chapter?

options.text: The command to keep the Sabbath, including not lighting a fire on that day.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 record this restated command.

options.text: The full list of the Ten Commandments.
options.note: Only the Sabbath command is restated here specifically, not the full Decalogue.

options.text: The instructions for the priestly garments only.
options.note: The garments are addressed later in the chapter's offering list; the opening restatement concerns the Sabbath.

options.text: Nothing was restated to the congregation.
options.note: Verses 1 through 3 explicitly restate the Sabbath command.

quiz.q: Who was invited to bring an offering for the tabernacle, according to verse 5?

options.text: Everyone whose heart was willing.
options.note: Verse 5 specifies this exact, voluntary condition for giving.

options.text: Only the tribe of Levi.
options.note: The offering was requested from the whole congregation of Israel, not the Levites alone.

options.text: Only the wealthiest families.
options.note: The invitation was based on willingness of heart, not wealth or social status.

options.text: No one specific group is mentioned.
options.note: Verse 5 explicitly specifies everyone whose heart was willing.

quiz.q: What specific skilled work did the women of Israel contribute, according to verses 25 to 26?

options.text: They spun blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, fine linen, and goat hair with their own hands.
options.note: Verses 25 to 26 describe this exact skilled contribution from the women.

options.text: They engraved the onyx stones for the ephod.
options.note: The leaders brought the onyx stones, verse 27; the women's specific contribution described here is spinning yarn and goat hair.

options.text: They built the wooden frames of the tabernacle.
options.note: The frame construction fell to Bezalel and the skilled craftsmen; the women's described work here is spinning.

options.text: No specific contribution from women is mentioned.
options.note: Verses 25 to 26 explicitly describe the women's skilled spinning.

quiz.q: What two abilities did God give Bezalel and Oholiab, according to verses 34 to 35?

options.text: Skill in craftsmanship and the ability to teach others.
options.note: Verse 34 specifically adds the ability to teach alongside their craftsmanship skill.

options.text: Wealth and political authority.
options.note: Their gifting concerned craftsmanship and teaching ability, not wealth or political power.

options.text: Prophetic insight and military strength.
options.note: Their described gifts are practical craftsmanship and teaching, not prophecy or military skill.

options.text: No specific abilities are described.
options.note: Verses 34 to 35 explicitly describe their craftsmanship and teaching abilities.

quiz.q: What kind of offering did the people bring, according to the repeated description in verses 21 and 29?

options.text: A freewill offering, brought by those whose hearts and spirits were stirred.
options.note: Both verses use this exact language of willing, spirit-prompted giving.

options.text: A mandatory tax assessed by tribal leaders.
options.note: The text explicitly emphasizes voluntary, heart-stirred giving, not a mandatory tax.

options.text: A single, one-time gift from Moses alone.
options.note: The offering came from the whole community, men and women together, not from Moses alone.

options.text: No offering was actually brought.
options.note: Verses 21 through 29 describe extensive, generous giving from the whole congregation.

questions: The people's hearts were stirred to give generously for the tabernacle, in sharp contrast to their earlier eager giving toward the golden calf. Where might your own generosity be currently directed toward the wrong things, and what would it look like to redirect it toward God?
Both men and women brought their skills and possessions freely for this work. What skills or resources has God given you that you have not yet offered willingly for His purposes?

Bezalel was given not only skill but the ability to teach others, multiplying his gift rather than keeping it to himself. Where do you have knowledge or ability you could be passing on to others rather than keeping for yourself alone?
So much was given that the offering eventually had to be restrained. What would need to change in your own giving for it to become this kind of overflowing, willing generosity?

God loves a cheerful giver, one who gives from a stirred heart rather than compulsion. Honestly examine your own giving, whether of money, time, or skill: does it flow more from willingness or from obligation?

translationNotes.note: Do not light a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day is a specific application of the general Sabbath rest command, likely addressing the labor involved in gathering fuel and tending a fire, later debated among Jewish interpreters regarding its exact scope.

Both men and women brought offerings, and the text specifically notes women's skilled spinning in verses 25 to 26, showing that the whole community, not merely male heads of households, participated directly in this work.

The ability to teach others, using a Hebrew root related to instruction, torah, shows that Bezalel and Oholiab's gifting was intended to be multiplied through others they trained, not confined to their own individual craftsmanship.
